title: San Sebastian Competition Title ‘Border’ Boards Reel Suspects for Global Sales (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Paris-based international sales company Reel Suspects has boarded worldwide sales on Chinese filmmaker Ah Biao’s feature debut “Border” (“Bian Jing”
body:
Paris-based international sales company Reel Suspects has boarded worldwide sales on Chinese filmmaker Ah Biao’s feature debut “Border” (“Bian Jing”), which will world premiere in the official selection of the San Sebastián Film Festival, where it competes for the Golden Shell.

	The cast includes Zheyan Li, Feng Qi, Sanming Han, Gang Zheng and Tao Guo, in a Hong Kong-U.S.-South Korea-Japan co-production. 


	The story centers on an impoverished young miner living a muted existence in a remote town where emotional reticence is the norm among men. A mysterious young woman disrupts his routine, awakening a curiosity he thought long dormant. Drawn to follow her into unfamiliar territory, he abandons the familiar comforts of his old life, not realizing she is hiding something about who she really is.
	

	“We’re thrilled to bring ‘Border’ to audiences at San Sebastián and to see the film presented in official competition,” said Matteo Lovadina, Reel Suspects CEO. “Ah Biao is a remarkable new voice with a distinctive cinematic vision, and we believe this is the beginning of a very exciting journey for him. He is undoubtedly a filmmaker to watch, and we’re delighted to be introducing his work to international audiences at such an important moment in his career. ‘Border’ presents a distinctive cinematic aesthetic rooted in Eastern experience. Through image, sound, performance and space, it draws on the language of cinema itself to explore the existential struggles of human experience. Its strikingly fresh audiovisual expression reveals another dimension of contemporary Chinese-language cinema.”
	

	Ah Biao, who was born in Shanxi, China, and is now based in Bangkok, works as a director, screenwriter and cinematographer. “Border” is his first feature, placing him in San Sebastián’s main competition lineup alongside veteran directors Mike Leigh, Pablo Larraín, Nicole Garcia and Yeşim Ustaoğlu.

	Borderless Films produced “Border,” with Jenny Man Wu as producer alongside fellow producers Lili Tong, Tyler Hill and Xue Ma. “For us, bringing a fully independently produced first feature to San Sebastián’s official competition is especially meaningful,” said producer Jenny Man Wu. “The film was carried forward by a deeply committed team who believed in Ah Biao’s vision and found ways to sustain it at every stage of its production.”

	The film also figures among 24 titles in the running for this year’s Sebastiane Award, an honor Basque LGBTIQA+ association Gehitu gives to the film judged the strongest portrayal of queer lives and experiences.

	Lovadina launched Reel Suspects in 2005 as a Paris-based boutique sales outfit specializing in independent film and up-and-coming directors, building an international reputation for elevated-genre fare alongside a roster of acclaimed first features and established names. The company’s current slate also includes Israel Cárdenas and Laura Amelia Guzmán’s “Interior Apartement Dia” and Zoe Berriatúa’s “Buffet Libre.”

schema.headline: San Sebastian Competition Title ‘Border’ Boards Reel Suspects for Global Sales (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Na Hong-Jin, Lav Diaz, Bertrand Mandico, Rintaro Headline Busan Master Class Lineup
description:
The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has unveiled the lineup for its Master Class, Cine Class and Special Talk programs.

	Master Class
body:
The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has unveiled the lineup for its Master Class, Cine Class and Special Talk programs.

	Master Class brings together four directors reflecting on their creative work. Na Hong-Jin, who drew global attention this year with “Hope,” will discuss the roots of his creative vision. Filipino auteur Lav Diaz and French director Bertrand Mandico, known for his distinctive visual style, round out the international side of the lineup. Japanese animation veteran Rintaro, director of “Galaxy Express 999” (1979) and “Metropolis” (2001), returns to Korea for the first time in 17 years.
	

	Cine Class, which launched last year, gathers six creators from different corners of the industry. Zhang Lu, winner of the Busan Award for Best Film at BIFF 2025 for “Gloaming in Luomu,” opens the program with reflections on cinema and life. Documentary filmmaker Seifollah Samadian will speak about his three-decade friendship with the late Iranian director Abbas Kiarostami. Judith Godrèche, whose public disclosures about abuse in the French film industry broke a long-standing silence and opened new space for women’s stories on screen, joins the lineup alongside producer Billy Acumen, whose credits include the “Roundup” franchise and “The King’s Warden” (2026). Director Bi Gan, recognized for his dreamlike visual approach since his debut, and actor Shim Eun-kyung, reflecting on a career that has crossed genres and borders, complete the session.


	Special Talk rounds out the programming with three conversations. Producer Kim Tae-ho, who recently moved into film acquisition and distribution, will appear alongside a screening of “Mother Mary” (2026). Ann Hui, this year’s Camellia Award recipient, will look back on her career in cinema. Film critic Jung Sung-il will lead a session tied to the Ahn Sung-ki tribute program, following a screening of “Festival” (1996), examining Korean film history through the late actor’s career.
	

	The 31st Busan International Film Festival will run Oct. 6-15 at the Busan Cinema Center and venues throughout Busan, with the 21st Asian Contents & Film Market held Oct. 10-13.

schema.headline: Na Hong-Jin, Lav Diaz, Bertrand Mandico, Rintaro Headline Busan Master Class Lineup

title: Jimmy Kimmel’s Pulled TV Interview With James Talarico Drops on YouTube as Texas Senate Candidate Says: ‘They’re Worried We’re Going to Win This Race’
description: Jimmy Kimmel turned to YouTube on Thursday night to house his interview with Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico — in light of fears th
body:
Jimmy Kimmel turned to YouTube on Thursday night to house his interview with Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico — in light of fears that the FCC would punish ABC stations for running the chat.

	“What are they so scared of you?” Kimmel asked the candidate. Said Talarico: “Well, they’re worried that we’re going to win this race in Texas. But we are the underdogs until the last vote is counted. We’re not just going up against the most corrupt politician in Texas. We’re going up against this entire corrupt system.”
	

	Among the topics that Kimmel and Talarico discussed were him not taking money from corporate PACs, Trump’s relationship with Talarico’s opponent (Ken Paxton), the GOP attempting to suppress voting and how the teachings of Jesus had been corrupted by the MAGA movement.


	“Scripture tells us that you can’t love God and hate other people,” Talarico said. “You can’t love God and abuse the immigrant. You can’t love God and oppress the poor. You can’t love God and bully the outcast … I was brought up to believe that in the face of a neighbor, we glimpse the face of God. Matthew 25 tells us Christians exactly how we’re going to be judged and how we’re going to be saved by feeding the hungry, by healing the sick, by welcoming the stranger. 

	“I often wonder what would Jesus do if he visited the U.S. Senate. I think he would tell the senators on the floor, ‘Depart from me, for I was hungry and you cut my food assistance. I was sick and you kicked me off Medicaid. I was a stranger and you deported me and my family.’ And then I think he would flip over those fancy desks on the floor of the U.S. Senate and demand that we take care of all of our neighbors, especially the least of these.”
	

	Talarico also addressed the fact that his opponent, Paxton, was previously impeached by his fellow Republicans for bribery. “Ken Paxton gets rich on the public’s dime, and then he refuses to answer basic questions about that corruption,” Talarico said. “I mean, literally, any time someone asks him a hard question, he runs away. You can watch these videos of people asking him about his 15 homes, asking him about the THC ban in Texas, and he gets this terrified look on his face, and he just walks the other way. When I get hard questions on the campaign trail, I answer them, and that’s exactly what we should expect from our public officials in a democracy.”

	On his actual ABC broadcast monologue Thursday, Kimmel told the audience that “this is — the show you’re watching — this is an unusual program for us because in a few minutes, I’m going to interview James Talarico — the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Texas. But you’re not going to see it.”

	Kimmel announced on his show Wednesday night that his interview with Talarico would not air on ABC and would instead be posted to YouTube, citing concerns about the FCC, which has previously threatened ABC station licenses and played a key role in Kimmel’s brief suspension in 2025.

	“Out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television,” Kimmel said. “It will be posted on YouTube instead. It will not be on TV.”

	He expanded on the reason in his Thursday monologue: “I mentioned last night, this interview will not be televised because of threats from the FCC, led by Commissioner Brendan Carr, who says we do not have the right to interview whichever candidates we want to interview. Which is something we’ve been doing for twenty-plus years.  

	“This is yet another attack on free speech, something that has become all too familiar for us here at the show for us in the country,” Kimmel added. “The FCC wants to make it impossible for me to interview candidates by requiring that I interview every candidate on the ballot who asks for equal time. So not only would I have to interview James Talarico as a Republican opponent, Ken Paxton — which, by the way, I would love to do, call me. I have many questions for you. Our affiliates in Texas would have to give equal time to as many candidates as there are on the ballot, and there’s about 10 candidates on the ballot. But the White House, once again, is claiming that what I’m saying, which is clearly true, is not true.
	

	“It’d be great news if we could do this the easy way instead of the hard way. That would be terrific.”

	Asked by MS NOW about the interview before it was posted to YouTube, Talarico said he was “still hopeful” it would air on ABC. He called the FCC’s threats “the most dangerous form of cancel culture,” saying, “People at the top, powerful politicians, powerful media executives, censoring what we watch, what we read, what we say. And that, again, should be a concern to everyone who believes in the First Amendment and believes in the freedom of speech.”

	It’s not the first time a late-night show has preempted an interview with the Texas Senate candidate. In February, Stephen Colbert said CBS executives pulled his interview with Talarico from the air over concerns about violating the FCC’s “equal time” rule, which requires broadcast stations to give equal time to political candidates when they appear on-air. While there are exemptions to the rule, Trump’s FCC chief Brendan Carr has been aggressive about clamping down on broadcast programs perceived as liberal. (The government agency is currently in a dispute with ABC’s “The View” and, in 2024, went after “Saturday Night Live” over a brief cameo by Kamala Harris.)

	Ultimately, Colbert put his Talarico interview on YouTube, with the clip garnering 9.5 million views. The Talarico campaign raised $2.5 million in the 24 hours after Colbert revealed he was barred from airing the interview.

	Here’s Kimmel’s interview with Talarico, posted Thursday night on YouTube:

schema.headline: Jimmy Kimmel’s Pulled TV Interview With James Talarico Drops on YouTube as Texas Senate Candidate Says: ‘They’re Worried We’re Going to Win This Race’

title: CBS Files Motion to Dismiss Former ‘Matlock’ Writer’s Lawsuit Alleging Racist, Sexist Comments: ‘We Stand Firmly Behind Our Producers’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: CBS Studios has filed a motion in Los Angeles Superior Court under the anti-SLAPP statute to strike a lawsuit filed earlier this summer by former “M
body:
CBS Studios has filed a motion in Los Angeles Superior Court under the anti-SLAPP statute to strike a lawsuit filed earlier this summer by former “Matlock” writer John Lowe. The CBS Studios filing included multiple declarations disputing his allegations against three of the show’s executive producers.

	Lowe’s suit against CBS Studios, showrunner Jennie Snyder Urman and executive producers Nicki Renna and Jeffrey Lieber alleged that “racially stereotyped comments about his body and genitalia” were made toward him and other Black cast and crew members, creating a “hostile work environment.”
	

	In its filing, the studio threw its full support behind Urman, Renna and Lieber, while countering many of Lowe’s allegations. Lowe’s attorney Ron Zambrano told Variety that they had not yet been served the motion yet, so he couldn’t comment on the specifics, while writing, “But I am confident we will successfully oppose the motion as the complaint was drafted with that possibility in mind.”


	“We take allegations of discrimination and harassment very seriously,” a CBS Studios spokesperson said. “Today, with the filing of our motion to strike, we took our first step toward challenging the baseless complaint filed by former ‘Matlock’ writer John Lowe. As stated in the motion and following a thorough investigation, we are confident that Lowe’s accusations are demonstrably inaccurate and maliciously fabricated, and will not allow them to go unchallenged.

	“False allegations are deeply damaging, both to those wrongly accused, and to anyone with a serious and legitimate claim of discrimination,” the spokesperson added. “We stand firmly behind our producers and look forward to the truth coming to light.” 
	

	In his lawsuit, Lowe — who worked on “Matlock” from October 2023 to July 2024 (as CBS Studios noted, not in 2025, as Lowe’s complaint stated) — claimed he was terminated from his position as a form of retaliation, as it came two weeks after reporting an alleged incident in which Urman referred to Juneteenth as “Coonteenth.”

	In declarations, Urman, Renna, Lieber and other witnesses disputed this, and said that Urman “never used that word (and) did not say it to Ms. Renna, to Lowe, or to anyone else.”

	Lowe had also in his complaint detailed an alleged incident claiming that Urman brought in her dog to the writers’ room, “citing that her children ‘didn’t like the aesthetic’ — referring to the dog’s black color.” He claimed he was coerced into taking the dog for nearly a year, while other staff were present, a move he felt “was racially motivated and designed to single him out for humiliation based on his race, not for any creative or production reason.”

	In declaration, Urman, Renna and Lieber said it wasn’t Urman’s dog, nor did she place it on Lowe’s lap or comment on the dog’s appearance, nor was she present when Lowe asked to adopt the dog.

	As for Lowe’s claims that Renna said Black cast member Eme Ikwuakor “can barely read” and allegedly called Lowe late at night and said she “was in bed wearing only her underwear,” the producers said in their declarations that Lowe made it up.

	And regarding Lowe’s allegations of sexually charged comments, the producers declared that “Lowe’s sexuality or his sex life was never questioned, nor was his body ever commented on.”

	Meanwhile, in her declaration, Urman said that in January 2026 — 18 months after his departure from “Matlock” — Lowe sent an email to Urman demanding $10,000. Urman said she reported the email to the company’s HR representative, and that Lowe’s first complaint to the company’s HR representative came after that demand for $10,000 and after Urman had contacted HR about it.

	Back in June, CBS Studios said it had investigated the allegations and didn’t find any merit to them: “We are committed to maintaining a safe and respectful environment for everyone and take all workplace complaints seriously,” a company spokesperson said at the time. “In this instance, a thorough investigation was completed, and we were unable to find support for his allegations. We look forward to vigorously defending this lawsuit.”
	

	At the same time, Lowe’s attorney, Ron Zambrano, sent this statement: “There is no excuse for this blatant racism and harassment. CBS should be ashamed for allowing it, and the ‘Matlock’ showrunner and producers should be held accountable. Mr. Lowe was subjected to degrading and unlawful conduct. He deserved to be treated with dignity and respect, as everyone should expect in the workplace, not subjected to these outrageous and illegal racial slurs and sexual harassment without any connection to his work on the show.”

	In the filing, CBS Studios said Lowe’s complaint was “filled with fabrications and outright lies that it resembles a grotesque work of fiction more than a court pleading. Lowe was never subjected to race or sex harassment as he claims, and as this case progresses, Defendants are confident that Plaintiff’s malicious and unsupported attacks will be publicly exposed for what they are: retaliation by a desperate man who was not renewed as a writer because his performance deficiencies detrimentally impacted CBS’ ability to convey the messages it desired.”

schema.headline: CBS Files Motion to Dismiss Former ‘Matlock’ Writer’s Lawsuit Alleging Racist, Sexist Comments: ‘We Stand Firmly Behind Our Producers’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: TIFF Opens With Siân Heder’s Crowd-Pleasing ‘Being Heumann’ — and Apple Has Its Next Oscar Contender
description: “Being Heumann” opens on a New York sidewalk that doesn’t allow Judy Heumann to climb it. There’s no curb cut or ramp. Just a woman and her wheelcha
body:
“Being Heumann” opens on a New York sidewalk that doesn’t allow Judy Heumann to climb it. There’s no curb cut or ramp. Just a woman and her wheelchair. Director Siân Heder holds on it — and then Judy gives the middle finger. And it immediately hooks the viewer in for the ride.

	At least that was the case for the audience inside Roy Thomson Hall, who sat with rapt attention as Heder’s film opened the 51st Toronto International Film Festival on Thursday night. The film is Heder’s first since “CODA,” the Sundance sensation which went on to win the best picture Oscar, a first for Apple Original Films and any streaming company. It chronicles the true story of how Heumann and her motley crew of activists fought for equal rights by waging a 28-day sit-in protest that helped pave the way for the Americans with Disabilities Act.
	

	”I don’t want to make a biopic about you. I want to make ‘Dog Day Afternoon’ with disabled people,” Heder said she told Heumann when she pitched herself to direct the project.


	After the screening — which ran with open captions, ASL interpreters and live captioning for the onstage portions — Heder sat for a Q&A with her actors to discuss how they made the film and her critical decision to cast actors with disabilities. Heder’s choice created a massive opportunity for actors like Madeley who has been a wheelchair user since birth.

	Madeley already idolized Heumann, known as the “Mother of the Disability Movement” — “She was funny. She was fierce. She was cheeky. She was naughty. She was sexy,” Madeley pointed out.
	

	“That is a gift for any actor to be able to play with all of those different things,” Madeleu continued. “But that was a challenge as well, and I knew the pressure that so many disabled people are waiting to see a character like this on the big screen, myself included.”

	The British actress — a BAFTA nominee for “Don’t Take My Baby,” and familiar to others from “Doctor Who” — has been very good in things you may have missed. Here she is the whole ballgame, and she plays Heumann without a single note of the saintly patience that biopics tend to hand their disabled subjects. Madeley’s Judy is funny, tactical, horny and even a little bit of an asshole sometimes. She is passionate about the right things and furious in a way that keeps finding new gears.

	The movie also shows what Heder can do with real money behind her. “CODA” was a small film about a small town, shot at the scale its budget allowed and beloved for its intimacy. “Being Heumann” is a period piece with a sprawling cast — the activists’ 28-day occupation of the San Francisco Federal Building, the longest occupation of a federal building in U.S. history, was staged with hundreds of people. From there, they bring their fight to Washington, D.C. and, finally, to secretary Joseph Califano’s front door. Apple funded the film, and Heder makes the leap look easy. Give a good director resources and you find out what she was doing without them.

	The ensemble around Madeley — Michael Patrick Thornton, Russell Harvard, Daniel Durant and a deep bench of disabled performers who describe themselves in the film as “radical crips” — is cast with an authenticity most productions still treat as a “nice-to-have.”

	“As disabled kids, you grow up being told like there’s this ceiling that’s made of vibranium that’s always hanging over you, and no matter what you do, you’re not going to be able to break out of this box, and confined to trying to do whatever society thinks that you can do,” said Charlie Rush-Reese, a blind performer who makes his acting debut in the film. “Being part of this project really not only inspired me to continue to chase my dreams and know that event a black kids in Minnesota can grow up to be in a movie like this, but … that [it] would inspire other disabled people to go out and chase their dreams.”
	

	Oscar nominee Mark Ruffalo, a decade after he brought “Spotlight” to Toronto, plays the bureaucrat stalling on Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act with the weary decency of a man who thinks the math is on his side. While he doesn’t have the role or screen time needed to propel his way into the supporting actor race, if the film gets big enough, you can never count him out.

	Dylan O’Brien, Rob Delaney and Ray Fisher round out the cast. 

	“My first thought when I signed up for the project was, ‘This would be such a fucking punk rock summer to be a part of,’” said O’Brien, who plays a local reporter who embeds himself with the activists and publicizes their efforts. But, making the movie was more meaningful than he anticipated. “Evan did not necessarily realize how galvanized he would be along with them, and that reflects my experience.”

	The film allows Heder to do something American movies rarely do. Without spoiling where the film goes, “Being Heumann” treats its disabled characters as full romantic and sexual beings: for example, there’s an intimate scene between a disabled performer and a nondisabled one that is played for tenderness and desire, not a learning lesson.

	Moreover, the film reinforces that that disability rights movement was never just about ramps and regulations for one community. It is, and has always been, about seeing this minority group as people who have the right to be wanted and not as a set of limitations someone else can see from across a room.

	The ultimate result is, plainly, a crowd-pleaser — the good kind — engineered by someone who knows the difference between manipulating its audience and bringing genuine care and heart to a story. It’s funny while also being inspiring, and specific without being alienating. That matters this weekend for one concrete reason and that’s the People’s Choice Award. Toronto’s audience vote carries more Oscar-season weight than any jury prize, and the pipeline is well-worn — “Nomadland,” “Green Book,” “12 Years a Slave.” If “Being Heumann” takes it, the conversation changes overnight from “Will it play?” to “How far can it go?”

	In the Oscars landscape, we can see a few possibilities. 

	Madeley belongs in the best actress discussion, and a win in Toronto would strengthen her position there. Screenplay is alive as well — Heder and Rebekah Taussig wrote from Heumann’s memoir, “Being Heumann: An Unrepentant Memoir of a Disability Rights Activist and Heder already owns an adapted screenplay Oscar for “CODA.”
	

	The film is a natural for the Academy’s casting category, given the scale and integrity of the ensemble Heder assembled. Add in production design with a 1977 New York, San Francisco and Washington, all rebuilt with period specificity.

	And best picture is not out of reach for a movie made by an Oscar-winning director, backed by the studio that won the category the last time she showed up at the big show.

	The campaign won’t have to manufacture that poignancy. The real Heumann died in 2023, having spent a lifetime making the country hold a door it kept trying to close. That message could be a strong factor.

	”Being Heumann” debuts in theaters on Nov. 6 before streaming on Apple TV.

schema.headline: TIFF Opens With Siân Heder’s Crowd-Pleasing ‘Being Heumann’ — and Apple Has Its Next Oscar Contender

title: J. M. Stelly’s Anatomica Films Taps Black Mandala for Global Sales on Horror Trio (EXCLUSIVE)
description: New Zealand’s Black Mandala has acquired worldwide sales rights to three horror films from Anatomica Films: “Within Madness,” “Vessel” and “The Thir
body:
New Zealand’s Black Mandala has acquired worldwide sales rights to three horror films from Anatomica Films: “Within Madness,” “Vessel” and “The Thirteenth Gate.” 

	J. M. Stelly wrote and directed all three, producing alongside Johnny Stassi through the Anatomica Films label.

	Stelly and Black Mandala co-founder Michael Kraetzer negotiated the agreement on Anatomica Films’ behalf.


	“Within Madness” draws on true events, tracing the fallout after filmmaker Mark Chapel and collaborator Donovan Summers are arrested. Investigators searching the case turn up human remains, execution tapes, Polaroids and film canisters cataloging years of violence. The evidence centers on “The Sacrament of Bondage,” a film capturing Summers’ spiral into brutality and his earliest killings. Prison interviews and recovered footage slowly reveal how deeply entangled the two men had become in their shared madness. Jared Bankens, Matt Story, Keegan Macy and Jamie Nipe star.
	

	“Vessel” follows Joseph, a pastor whose faith crumbles after his wife, Mary, goes missing and their unborn child is lost. Retracing the days leading up to her disappearance, Joseph experiences past and present blurring together, while escalating disturbances in their home point to something far more sinister than grief. What starts as a portrait of grief ultimately reveals an entity trying to cross into the world through human suffering. Keegan Macy, Jamie Nipe and Dane Rhodes are featured.

	“The Thirteenth Gate” centers on investigator Nathan Hale, who regains consciousness inside a derelict industrial complex without knowing how he got there. While hunting for his missing wife, Marissa, Hale is dragged through an escalating nightmare of environments that loop, warp and rebuild themselves from his own memories and trauma. Behind the ordeal is an enigmatic figure called M, orchestrating an occult ritual designed to unlock thirteen gates into the ethereal plane. The deeper Hale goes into the labyrinth, the harder it becomes to separate physical reality from memory and constructed experience. The film moves like an immersive, POV-driven psychological horror trip that blends body horror, occult mythology and science-fiction touches. Jeff Pearson, Jamie Nipe and Keegan Macy round out the cast.
	

	“We’re incredibly happy to be working with such an outstanding and unique filmmaking talent and look forward to building the international success of these very special titles together,” Kraetzer said. He added that each film carries its own distinctive atmosphere, vision and identity, calling the collaboration a chance to work with bold, original filmmaking that he believes can connect with genre audiences, festivals, platforms and buyers around the world.

	“We’re proud to welcome ‘Vessel,’ ‘Within Madness’ and ‘The Thirteenth Gate’ to the Black Mandala lineup,” he said, “and are very much looking forward to presenting these films internationally, building their worldwide audience, and developing a successful long-term collaboration with the filmmaker.”

	Stelly said he was pleased to have Black Mandala representing the films, noting that “these intensely personal projects each explore horror from a very different perspective.” He pointed to Black Mandala’s track record building an international presence around bold genre filmmaking and said he is looking forward to working with the company’s team to bring the films to audiences around the world.

	“Within Madness” will be the first of the three to go before buyers, launching sales at the Toronto Film Festival market before all three titles are pitched to buyers at AFM. 

	Stelly is represented by Zero Gravity Management.

schema.headline: J. M. Stelly’s Anatomica Films Taps Black Mandala for Global Sales on Horror Trio (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Being Heumann’ Review: Siân Heder’s First Film Since ‘CODA’ Is a Bold and Stirring Dramatization of the Protest That Launched the Disabled-Rights Revolution
description: There’s a quality that liberal social-protest dramas tend to have in common. They’re usually about revolutionary moments we’ve come through and are
body:
There’s a quality that liberal social-protest dramas tend to have in common. They’re usually about revolutionary moments we’ve come through and are on the other side of, so they can encourage the audience to feel — with a touch of sanctimony — that yesterday’s revolution was never anything but today’s common sense. That’s been true of many movies, even some fine ones, about the Civil Rights movement or the gay rights movement. It’s true, as well, of a movie about the fight for union rights like “Norma Rae.”
	

	But when you watch “Being Heumann,” a drama about the astonishing 1977 protest that launched the disability-rights revolution (it opened the Toronto International Film Festival tonight), the film doesn’t give you that sanctimonious “Oh, of course” feeling. That’s because the director, Siân Heder, who made a splash five years ago with “CODA” (this is the first film she’s made since), takes pains to preserve, as emotion and drama, the radicalism of what the movie is about.


	“Being Heumann” features a cast of disabled actors playing disabled people, and the actors have a raw, piercing, in-your-face quality that burns away any hint of sentimental complacency. But Heder uses the authenticity of her casting in a super-sly, double-edged way. She’s following up on what she did in “CODA,” where she placed deaf actors like Troy Kotsur at the center of her story in a way that mainstream movies almost never had. The humanity of her characters transcended their disabilities — yet in a way that’s too simple, since the movie insisted on how central the disabilities were to their identities. In addition to telling a great story, “CODA” busted through our pieties about how we characterize people.
	

	“Being Heumann” isn’t as transporting a movie as “CODA” was, yet it’s a stirring drama cut from the same cloth of cathartic empathy. And it’s also structurally bold. The movie chronicles a sit-in, sparked by the disabled-rights leader Judy Heumann (Ruth Madeley), that lasted for 28 days, as Huemann and her fellow protesters entered the Federal Building in San Francisco to confront the officials there, and wound up staying in the building — not because they’d planned it that way, but because that’s how the situation evolved. They were rolling with the punches, the politics, the media, and their own desperate impacted lives of messed-up righteousness. They wouldn’t take no for an answer, and “no” was the only answer they were getting. What they were fighting for was nothing less than the right to be treated — and seen — as full human beings.

	Heder echoes the spontaneity of that journey, and mirrors it in how the film invites us to relate to its inspiringly prickly ensemble. The performances have a casual purity, and are often quite forceful, yet when the protesters first come together and we’re getting to know them, there’s a part of us that surveys them and says: Look, it’s a person with MS. It’s a blind person. It’s a deaf person. It’s a woman in a wheelchair. It’s a man wearing a brace on his head attached to a plastic orb he uses to tap out letters to say words. At first, the film all but inevitably encourages us to define each character by his or her disability — and the moment we’ve done that, we’ve actually tumbled, without realizing it, down a small rabbit hole of prejudice.

	The movie opens in 1972, when Judy, in New York City, leads an early protest, all to try to get the government to pass Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, an anti-discriminatory measure that will guarantee the rights of disabled people to take part in all programs that receive federal funding. (That, of course, is most of American life.) Heder, who has a sixth sense for how to place the camera in a way that’s subjective and electrifying, introduces Judy, who’s been disabled since she was a child and is in a wheelchair, as she’s making her way through the puddles of midtown Manhattan (with Iggy Pop’s “The Passenger” on the soundtrack), experiencing herself as an encumbrance. When she reaches the building her protest is organized to stand in front of, the whole event (the protesters chanting “Sign 504!”) falls on deaf ears. So she says “Let me down,” meaning down into the street, and she then wheels herself out there and stops a Mack truck right in the middle of Madison Ave. That’s Judy Heumann. As played by Ruth Madeley, who looks like Bonnie Hunt but acts like an officious Joan of Arc, she’s hellbent on gaining the human rights that no one apart from disabled people seems to realize they don’t have.
	

	Cut to five years later. It’s 1977, and Section 504 has been passed into law by the U.S. Congress; it passed by a few votes from people who, the movie suggests, barely knew what they were doing. Nevertheless: a victory, right? Not quite. Section 504 will not become law until Joseph Califano, the U.S. Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare under President Jimmy Carter, signs it into law. And he’s hedging; he doesn’t want to do it. Why not?

	This is where the film becomes morally captivating. Carter was the most dogged liberal president of the last 60 years, and Califano — played with weary mid-century bureaucratic testiness by Mark Ruffalo — was a veteran ally of the Civil Rights movement who, in spirit, is very much a card-carrying liberal. Yet he’s a stubbornly conventional one. For him, it’s all about the money — and if Section 504 passes, it will mean that everything from schools to buses to sidewalks will have to be made over to accommodate the needs of disabled people. He says that will cost $2.4 billion (in 1977, an astronomical sum). He says: We can’t afford it. But what he means is (and this is the non-liberal side of liberalism): We can’t afford it just for those people.

	Judy Heumann, living in San Francisco, is helping to organize a nationwide series of protests by disabled people against the oppression they’ve been living under. Section 504 is now law; they just want the HEW Secretary to sign it. Yet what they’re really fighting is the oppression of being treated as cripples — a hard-wired social prejudice that dictates, quite often, that they can’t go to school or get a job. (Judy talks about how they wouldn’t let her into school until she was 10 because she was considered a “fire hazard.” Which is often the excuse.) And the only way they’ll be able to do any of those things is if the federal government coughs up the money because it understands what disabled people need to live a full life: ramps that go alongside stairways, cut curbs that provide spaces for wheelchairs, and the demand that educators, and employers, do not look at disabled people and see a problem but, rather, a person with all the potential that implies.

	This is a true upsurge in consciousness, reinforced by how we come to embrace the humanity of everyone onscreen. Judy has gathered up protesters with many different disabilities, and at one point we see how their priorities clash. The sit-in at the San Francisco Federal Building, which was the longest in U.S. history, takes its spirit from the Civil Rights movement, and from Gandhi too, when Judy goes on a hunger strike. One of the protesters, Brad Lomax (Antwan Tolliver), is a Black Panther, and his Panther comrades help out, bringing food to sustain the journey. Yet what’s dramatic and at times scaldingly funny about “Being Huemann” is how the characters’ fury brings them to life, whether it’s Kitty (Madeline Delp) turning her librarian personality inside out or Hale (Andrew Pilkington) tapping out the eloquence of his anger. Judy Heumann truly sparked a revolution, though it would be 13 years before the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 was signed into law. And as “Being Heumann” captures with subversive gusto, the real disability revolution — the one in which we look at someone with a disability and just see another person in front of us — is still a work in progress.

schema.headline: ‘Being Heumann’ Review: Siân Heder’s First Film Since ‘CODA’ Is a Bold and Stirring Dramatization of the Protest That Launched the Disabled-Rights Revolution

title: ‘Burgundy’ Review: An Attractive, Light-Bodied Wine Doc With a Good Nose but No Legs
description: “Everything that follows is true. Exactly as we dreamed it,” reads the opening title of “Burgundy,” from award-winning documentary duo Michael Dweck
body:
“Everything that follows is true. Exactly as we dreamed it,” reads the opening title of “Burgundy,” from award-winning documentary duo Michael Dweck and Gregory Kershaw, with an almost legible wink. It’s a sweet start to a sweet movie, but in retrospect it sounds a little defensive, as though the pair are aware that, especially compared to their last two lovely films — 2020’s “The Truffle Hunters” and 2024’s “Gaucho Gaucho” — “Burgundy” feels less like an incisive portrait of a particular arcane lifestyle than a rambling reverie about it. Amiably riffing on the viticultural tradition of the eponymous winemaking region of eastern-central France, “Burgundy” has more fragrance than substance and even then, too quickly loses its bouquet. 
	

	If dream it is, however, it’s a pleasant one — no night terrors in these terroirs — especially given that the directors, who are also responsible for the scrumptious cinematography, find so much material for their trademark, eye-catchingly pictorialist visuals. As perky ’60s pop songs play, perfectly composed chateaux-tableaux that are so crowded with billiard tables, oil paintings and antique tchotchkesthey feel like slightly sardonic wealth critique, we are first introduced to Bertrand Devillard, patriarch of a winemaking estate that dates back 160 years. Bertrand is a hands-on boss, and even when relaxing by the pool or doing a little skeet shooting, a worried one. His grandson Melchior is more interested in the world of high finance than in taking over the family business that would naturally be his inheritance. 


	That there would be plenty of people from outside the clan willing to step into that breach is proven by Enzo, a handsome young man with the throwback good looks of a midcentury matinee idol (he self-consciously models himself after his hero, Jean Gabin) whose ambition is one day to run his own vineyard. For the time being he comes to work on Bertrand’s estate, learning the ropes from the bottom up — cleaning the massive vats, stomping the season’s harvest, sampling wines he could never otherwise afford in an effort to educate his palate. Amusingly sketch-like intros then round out the rest of the cast, which includes Enzo’s eventual girlfriend, Céleste, a trainee sommelier; Patrick, the maitre’d of a nearby 3-Michelin-Star restaurant; and Guillaume, a recently separated wine critic whose adventures in dating, therapy and physio (for RSI due to lifting 100 glasses a day) make him the droll comic relief in a film whose tone is rarely serious enough to need relieving. 
	

	As in their other feature docs, Dweck and Kershaw’s craftsmanship is superb — they’re at least as meticulous and detail-oriented as their proudly finicky subjects. And the deliberately stilted restaging of interactions that likely originally happened in a much less picturesque manner is an inextricable part of their approach. So too are editor Pauline Gaillard’s sharp cuts, which are often timed exactly to coincide with the moment that someone lost in faraway thought finishes swirling their mouthful of Pinot Noir and hocks it unceremoniously into a nearby receptacle. 

	Less successfully, this time out the directors further break strict documentary protocol by including some whimsical 8mm footage, usually of Enzo and Céleste’s burgeoning relationship, which is again nicely shot but feels reversed in, as though it was only included as filler when the actual storylines were found to be getting bit sparse. An entire sequence in which the pair go to the movies to watch “Bonnie and Clyde” and then enact their own heist as pastiche versions of Faye Dunaway and Warren Beatty, is just a bit too cute and a digression too far from the film’s ostensible topic.

	“The Truffle Hunters” followed several leathery Piedmontese old-timers and their absurdly touching relationships with their truffle-snuffling dogs. “Burgundy,” by contrast, has no natural source of such effortless, warm-hearted charm and without it, the portraiture sometimes veers closer to caricature. Perhaps for the first time, the limitations of Dweck and Kershaw’s deliberate, constructed style make themselves felt: when messy real life intrudes, the film rather flounders. Enzo abruptly goes off-script, so to speak, and quits the Devillard estate to try his hand at mussel farming and pouf! The narrative of a dedicated striver following his long-cherished dream evaporates at the revelation that maybe his lifelong fascination with viticulture was not so lifelong after all. 

	The filmmakers hastily shift course and retool the final third of “Burgundy” as a kind of star cross’d lovers romance, when Céleste also quits her apprenticeship and moves to Paris, and the young, sundered couple can be portrayed as pining for one another. Not only is this pivot a little hard to invest in, given we’ve been burned before, more grievously, it takes the main focus of the action away from the very region and wine culture the film is purportedly celebrating. 
	

	It is possible that true wine experts will respond to those parts of “Burgundy” that unabashedly ennoble the various different disciplines within the wine arts. Film lovers, on the other hand might be left unsatisfied by an approach that strains the limits of documentary realism to no particular end, save to further mythologize an already singularly rarefied sphere. And even if “Burgundy” is for oenophiles rather than cinephiles, presumably they too will be a little let down by a vintage that is fruity and full of promise at the first sip, but that loses its complexity — if not its easy drinkability — long before the last.

title: ‘Stuffed’ Review: Jodie Comer and Harry Melling Sing the Body Eccentric in an Odd, and Oddly Touching, Taxidermy Musical
description: It’s a somewhat telling coincidence that “Stuffed,” a very peculiar new vehicle for Jodie Comer, is premiering at the same edition of Toronto as “Pr
body:
It’s a somewhat telling coincidence that “Stuffed,” a very peculiar new vehicle for Jodie Comer, is premiering at the same edition of Toronto as “Prima Facie,” the film adaptation of the stage hit that won the Liverpudlian actor a Tony last year, but with Cynthia Erivo taking over her role for the screen. “Prima Facie” could have given Comer a chance to dazzle a wider audience with what we already knew she could do; “Stuffed” will delight and/or bewilder a smaller one with what we definitely didn’t, namely Broadway-level musical emoting in a macabre pop-opera about a romance unfolding through the art of taxidermy. She scores points for risk-taking, then, but she also just scores: A high-wire high-concept piece like this stands or falls by the conviction that the actors bring to it, and Comer plays it from the gut.
	

	So, for that matter, does Harry Melling — an actor who, following last year’s sub-dom romcom of sorts “Pillion,” seems to be making unlikely British indie love stories his niche. Which makes sense, given that he’s a pretty unlikely leading man: His slightly crumpled face, with its resting expression of forlorn, puppyish vulnerability, carries much of the comedy and the tragedy in Theo Rhys‘ endearingly bizarre debut feature, adapted and expanded from his BAFTA-nominated short of the same name. It’s those disarranged features and disconsolate mien that make his character, friendless factory drone Bernie, a figure of fascination for hermetic amateur taxidermist Araminta (Comer); she likes them so much, in fact, that she’d like to fix them in place forever.
	

	In its briefest form, the logline for “Stuffed” promises body horror of the most morbid order: A woman obsessed with the idea of forever preserving a human body advertises for a volunteer to be killed and made into a fleshly artwork; a man who feels invisible while he’s alive steps forward, believing that once he’s stuffed, he’ll finally be seen. David Cronenberg could have done something vividly disturbing and intimately sensual with this idea, but it’s unlikely the result would have landed anywhere in the ballpark of “sweet” — which Rhys’ film, against substantial odds, actually is, even as its atmosphere of fetid physical and psychological decay turns the stomach a little. 

	If making the whole enterprise a musical sounds like something of a tongue-in-cheek stunt, meanwhile, that’s reckoning without the plaintive lyricism of writer-composer Joss Holden-Rea’s songcraft, which feels heavily indebted to the earnest modern school of Broadway balladry. The score could use a few more hummable tunes, but its sincerity is welcome in a film so rooted in extreme strangeness that it needs to dial down the quirk factor in at least a couple of areas. 

	Indeed, “Stuffed” takes some time to find a happy medium between the violent eccentricity of its premise and its potential for positively baroque levels of British tweeness. Its opening passages lean in the latter direction, outlining Bernie’s humdrum existence (complete with perfectly banal job in a sandwich factory) with fairytale-style naïveté to match his unworldly outlook, not to mention a hint of Wes Anderson stylization in the superb production design by Beck Rainford (“Ray and Liz,” “Club Zero”), albeit with a thrift-store scruffiness and perennially overcast backdrop to suit the film’s working-class Northern setting. (Rainford also provides ample sight gags for any viewers still tickled by the “bad taxidermy” meme that ruled the web a few years back.)

	Once we getting into the more granular details of these people’s lives, however, they start ringing a little more true — and so in turn does the film. A socially awkward introvert devoted to the single mother who, it seems, raised him well into adulthood, Bernie is now returning her care as she slips into dementia — but when she stops recognizing him, it’s as if his sole connection with another human being has been snuffed out. Araminta, it gradually emerges, has a different backstory behind her withdrawal from the world, though her introversion is of a more confidently, creatively aloof variety. When Bernie responds to her ad, he’s astonished that someone so interesting and witchily beautiful should have designs on his body, even if those designs involve formaldehyde: She practically flatters him into a death wish.
	

	Yet the more time they spend together, mapping out their exact plans for his demise and preservation, the more they appear to be peas in one very lonely pod, and mutual intrigue turns to affection. Where does that leave the gruesome project that binds them together? Rhys and Holden-Rea’s script — deftly and quite knottily expanded from the story’s shorter format — takes the central relationship through stages that nod, by turns, to the odd-couple romanticism of Richard Curtis and the knife-twisting adult storytelling of Roald Dahl, with a final dose of Shakespearean fatalism for good measure.

	None of which would convince if Comer and Melling weren’t so honestly committed to the bit. Both quite capable singers, they’re alive to the kitsch excesses of the film’s horror, melodrama and musicality, not to mention Holly Rebecca’s suitably mothballed costumes. But they play it just straight enough too: Together, they find a deep, calcified sadness to these oddballs, a desperate need to do something, anything extraordinary, and, finally, a giddy flicker of empathetic self-recognition in each other. It’s that sadness, and that relief, that ultimately dignifies them and their demented mission — and that makes “Stuffed” a more poignant ode to human embalming than anyone might have thought possible.

title: Oscar Predictions 2027: Telluride Reshapes the Best Picture Race as TIFF Lines Up Its Crowd-Pleasers
description:
Sep 10, 2026 8:40pm PT	
	

	
	Oscar Predictions 2027: Telluride Reshapes the Best Picture Race as TIFF Lines Up Its Crowd-Pleasers
body:
Sep 10, 2026 8:40pm PT	
	

	
	Oscar Predictions 2027: Telluride Reshapes the Best Picture Race as TIFF Lines Up Its Crowd-Pleasers
	



			
			
	
						

									Courtesy of VIFF
	
					


							
		

	Variety Awards Circuit section is the home for all awards news and related content throughout the year, featuring the following: the official predictions for the upcoming Oscars, Emmys, Grammys and Tony Awards ceremonies, curated by Variety chief awards editor Clayton Davis. The prediction pages reflect the current standings in the race and do not reflect personal preferences for any individual contender. As other formal (and informal) polls suggest, competitions are fluid and subject to change based on buzz and events. Predictions are updated every Thursday.



	

					Steve Buscemi and Sam Rockwell in WILD HORSE NINE. Photo by Searchlight Pictures/Diego Araya Corvalán, Courtesy of Searchlight Pictures. © 2026 Searchlight Pictures. All Rights Reserved.
									Searchlight Pictures
	




	2027 Academy Awards Predictions Commentary All Categories (Updated: Sept. 10, 2026): The presumed best picture front-runner will not screen for another three months. The other one has been playing since July. And then there’s everything in between.

	“Dune: Part Three” won’t arrive until December, and Denis Villeneuve’s finale will hang over every projection between now and then. Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” opened in the summer and has not slipped an inch since. Neither felt any need to haul itself up to any of the festivals. 

	The movies that actually turned up in Telluride are why the race reads differently this week than it did last. Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine,” with John Malkovich doing the loosest, meanest work of his late career, walked out of its first screening to the kind of ovation that puts him and the movie, squarely in the thick of the race. Searchlight has made this climb before, and they have their eye on the prize. Over at Focus Features, Simon Stone’s “Elsinore” handed Andrew Scott a showcase that the awards team can build a whole campaign around. A24’s “The Debut” had the biggest applause at the fest, and now TIFF will digest it and see if it can go even further.

	But A24 has other stuff up its sleeves.

	No documentary has ever been nominated for best picture. Not saying there haven’t been worthy entrants such as “Hoop Dreams,” “Searching for Sugar Man” and dozens of others. Across nearly a hundred years of this ceremony, the category has kept a wall between nonfiction and the top prize and that wall has never once come down. Enter Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s “You Can See Everything,” which surprised Telluride and took the town by storm. If the film holds through the fall, the 99th Academy Awards could hand a documentary feature the first pest picture nomination in Oscar history and A24 wants it.

	Then there is “Wildwood,” which was just announced as the opening night film of AFI Fest and Laika is looking to make its own history.

	Three animated films have ever broken through into the top category. “Beauty and the Beast.” “Up.” “Toy Story 3.” Every last one of them representing a Disney flag. Laika, the Oregon studio that has spent two decades building whole worlds one agonizing frame at a time, has never come within shouting distance of the marquee category. Travis Knight’s “Wildwood” is the film that could finally get there, and getting there would make Laika the first animation house from outside the Disney orbit to land in the category. A stop-motion fantasy, hand-posed frame by frame, could go the distance.

	But first, Toronto will get its say. While Telluride is a room full of believers, TIFF is tens of thousands of strangers with a ballot and its People’s Choice Award that can prove that a movie has what it takes. 

	The predictions will look nothing like this by Thanksgiving, and we’re ready to keep watching the race unfold.

	The Governors Awards, which will hand out honorary Oscars to Glenn Close and Ridley Scott, will take place Sunday, Nov. 15. Preliminary voting for the Oscars shortlist in 12 categories runs Dec. 7-11, with the shortlist announcement to follow Tuesday, Dec. 15. Following the close of the eligibility period on Dec. 31, 2026, nominations voting will run Jan. 11-15, 2027. The official Oscar nominations will be announced on Thursday, Jan. 21, 2027. The 99th Oscars will take place on Sunday, March 14, 2027 and will be hosted by Conan O’Brien. The ceremony airs live at 7 p.m. ET on ABC and in more than 200 territories worldwide from the Dolby Theatre at Ovation Hollywood.

title: President Trump Goes Off on ABC News Reporter Over $40 Trillion Debt Question
description:
President Trump
                          Screams At ABC News Reporter, 'Not You'!!!
body:
President Trump
                          Screams At ABC News Reporter, 'Not You'!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 11, 2026
                            1:20 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            President Trump laid into an ABC News reporter who dared to ask him a question related to the $40 trillion national debt — and the shocking moment was all caught on camera.
      
    
            Trump took questions from reporters on the tarmac after he landed in Dallas, Texas, to attend Thursday night's Republican National Convention — and things got really tense when ABC's Rachel Scott fired off a zinger about our whopping national debt.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            In the clip, Scott asks Trump why he needs to offer each American a $5,000 check to incentivize them to vote in the midterms if his economic policies are working, suggesting the prez is simply buying votes.
      

            Trump denies that he's incentivizing voters, claiming he's only rewarding them after having to endure 4 years of bad economic policies during the Biden administration that bled into the first part of his second term in office.  Trump also blasted Biden's policies on crime and the border.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            When Scott tried to ask a follow up question, that's when Trump just lost it and repeatedly snapped at her, sneering, "Not you!" Trump also leaned into Scott with fury in his face.
      
    
            It's no shock that Trump yelled at a reporter ... he's been doing that for years ... but watch the clip ... it's worth it.

schema.headline: President Trump Goes Off on ABC News Reporter Over $40 Trillion Debt Question

title: Man Charged After Infant Son Dies After Being Left in Hot Car
description:
Connecticut Father
                          Allegedly Left Infant Son Alone in Hot Car
body:
Connecticut Father
                          Allegedly Left Infant Son Alone in Hot Car
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 10, 2026
                            5:50 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A Connecticut man is being charged after allegedly leaving his infant son in a hot car ... and the boy later died.
      
    
            The East Windsor Police Department says they got a call from Kevin Pell last month, who told them he had left the boy in the car because he had been sleeping.
      
    
            Pell had gone to work on his family's strawberry farm while the 1-year-old was in the car. He allegedly told police he came back to find the boy "blue and not breathing."
      

            According to a search warrant obtained by PEOPLE, the father allegedly told the dispatcher that he "didn’t have the AC on" in the car ... but switched up and said it had been on when the cops arrived.
      
    
            The warrant says the car was "not habitable for the child" ... because it had been parked directly in the sun with the windows and sunroof closed.
      
    
            Police say Pell had been performing CPR on the baby when first responders arrived and took over.
      
    
            The child was brought to Connecticut Children's Medical Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
      
    
            Pell has been charged with risk of injury to a child ... and may face additional charges as the investigation continues.
      
    
            He appeared in court Thursday but didn't enter a plea. Pell's due back in court next month.

            A 5th plane was targeted by terrorists on 9/11 -- something the government does not want you to know -- so says the pilot, the flight attendants, the airline's dispatcher, and others.
      
    
            TMZ produced a documentary -- "TMZ Investigates 9/11: The Fifth Plane" -- which is currently on YouTube. The doc described the events on United Flight 23, which was scheduled to take off from JFK at 9:00 AM, with Los Angeles as the final destination.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            There were 7 people who raised suspicion on the part of the crew, checking out the cockpit, arguing with a flight attendant not to delay the takeoff over a food issue.
      

            There's hard evidence people were hiding in the hatch of the plane ... only to surface after the plane was evacuated and locked ... presumably looking to recover incriminating evidence.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The FBI secretly interviewed the entire flight crew, and even presented them with a lineup.
      
    
            Yet Flight 23 became a deep, dark secret ... the government, the FBI, and United Airlines have all been radio silent.
      
    
            Watch "TMZ Investigates 9/11: The Fifth Plane" ... on YouTube.

            Sept 11, 2001 -- a day the nation will never forget. A day thousands of emergency responders and civilians risked their lives to save others. A day when the nation came together in the face of unimaginable tragedy ...
      
    
            25 years after the Twin Towers in New York City were struck by hijacked American Airlines Flight 11 and United Airlines Flight 175, we remember the nearly 3,000 lives lost, we honor those affected, and we never forget the lives lost and the devastation of that day.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The harrowing photos from that tragic Tuesday captured moments of unimaginable fear, heartbreak, and courage.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The Pentagon was also targeted that morning, when American Airlines Flight 77 was hijacked and crashed into the building, killing 184 people.
      
    
            We also remember the 44 lives lost on United Airlines Flight 93 that was also hijacked but crashed into a field in Pennsylvania.
      
    
            Twenty-five years later, these powerful images remain a haunting reminder of the lives lost and the selfless bravery of those who rushed to help.
      
    
            Look back at these unforgettable images.
